The foundation of corporate influence in television is the overhead of production value. Like any industry, or any form of publishing, television has a 'marginal cost'. A cost for making the episodes of the show. This cost is keyed to production value. The better the production looks, the nicer the sets and special effects, the better the video technology, the more exotic the filming locations, and the better and more well known the actors the more it all costs. As long as people are drawn to a high production value, and that production value costs a lot of money, it will take large speculative investment to produce each 'run' of episodes for the show. And so the production company/TV network must sell the eyeballs of the audience to corporations to cover the cost of production. Advertizing. Once a show has been established for a season or so, the TV network can collect demographics on the show and use that information to sell to advertisers. But when a show is brand new, the first series production is speculative. Either the network itself must speculate on the production themselves--which they often don't have the money for--or key anchor advertisers are invited in to consider the show. Thus we have 'pilot' episodes; introductory episodes of a new show made to sell the concept to prospective advertisers and test audiences. And these advertisers are inclined to support shows whose content they think reflects favorably on the image of their companies and products. The networks and production companies know this and so they will subtly tailor their programs to accommodate that. They will also do this with established shows when they notice that advertisers are more or less interested in advertising on that show.

This kind of influence has always been considered controversial and potentially corrupting, particularly when it comes to the broadcast of news and events. Governments were always concerned about a corporate worldview becoming dominant on TV and potentially influencing public opinion and the political process. And commercial TV always ignored things like educational and public service programming. So, in an attempt to balance things out, many nations developed government-sponsored TV where shows were financed on a fixed annual budget and where they, ostensibly, would be free of influence by corporate interests. This has taken three basic forms; publicly sponsored TV networks where programming was financed by viewer subscriptions, national TV networks financed by the government (or more usually a combination of government and private donations), and public access TV limited to local areas where the general public could access the production studios and make their own simple TV shows. Generally, the production value of programming for this kind of TV has been consistently poorer because government simply would never put up the kind of money required. But this began to improve as artistic and educational foundations created by the wealthy began donating to their programming, particularly for children's education and science and nature documentaries.

But, of course, there's a hazard in this too as government bureaucrats and wealthy patrons could influence the content of shows because they're the ones writing the checks. In more despotic countries national TV has often been reduced to a pure propaganda instrument and independent TV networks barred or suppressed. In recent years right-wing pundits and politicians have targeted public TV for criticism and defunding because they feel its content is left-biased. This may well be, since there are no rich people working in public TV, they tend to come out of the academic and artists communities, and they certainly aren't concerned with profit or what rich people think or they would leave for commercial TV.

In recent years several phenomenon have emerged to disrupt how TV works, functionally and economically. Cable networks emerged, which had the effect of allowing TV production companies to become more independent of the traditional networks. You can now form a production company around a show, independently produce pilot episodes, and sell it cable companies, networks, advertisers, and private philanthropic on your own. There is a regular convention circuit for this. Many reality TV shows came out of this phenomenon as well as animated shows. Since pilots have to be financed out-of-pocket for these production companies, they must seek individual investors to do that initial production.

Then came the Internet and a variety of streaming platforms. This has so far been limited to being an alternative to local public access TV, giving people the power to reach the world with their own crude home-made TV shows. But technology is now eroding the overhead of some aspects of production value. High quality video is becoming relatively cheap and CGI is lowering the bar for special effects. So you now have some remarkable programming made by so-called amateurs and volunteers. Take, for example, Star Trek Continues; a YouTube series deriving from the original Star Trek that is fully on-par with the production value of the original TV series, but fan-made entirely by amateurs and vollunteers. This would have been unthinkable ten years ago. And programs like this have promising new channels of public funding and sponsorship; Kickstarter and Patreon. However, none of these have ever reached the kind of crowdfunded sponsorship that could cover the cost of productions that are in the area of millions of dollars per episode, as we commonly see in commercial TV. Many kinds of TV programming don't need a lot of overhead in production value if they are sufficiently creative in content. The rise of reality TV was not based on production value but the novelty of the concept --though that novelty quickly wore-off as too many producers jumped on it because it was so cheap to do and wore it out. But you're not yet going to produce things like Game of Thrones from crowdfunding.

For the time being, as long as people want programming that requires millions of dollars per episode to create, or news that takes a big infrastructure with a lot of people, it's going to take upper-class gatekeepers of money to make them possible, be they rich philanthropists, corporate CEOs, or apparatchiks. And we can only rely on their ethics when it comes to their minimizing their influence on content.

If you want to reduce corporate influence in TV, then you have to give your eyeballs, your own money, and maybe even your own volunteer effort to the real independents. To the people who make TV out of love. This is why I've always been a fan of public access TV and the DIY internet shows. I grew up watching things like the Uncle Floyd Show and Biker Billy Cooks With Fire. More recently, the many community-made things on YouTube and the more independent video stream services. I don't even have a TV anymore.
